text: Hermitian operators represent things you measure. Unitary operators represent something different but just as fundamental: the ways a quantum state is allowed to evolve over time, including every gate in a quantum circuit.

A matrix U is unitary if its conjugate transpose is also its inverse — U dagger U equals the identity. One direct consequence: the inner product of two transformed vectors equals the inner product of the originals, always. A unitary transformation can rotate a vector around in the space, but it can never stretch, shrink, or change the overlap between two vectors.

The Hadamard matrix is 1 over the square root of 2, times 1,1,1, negative 1 — one of the most common single-qubit gates. Since every entry is real and the matrix is symmetric, H dagger equals H itself, so checking H dagger H means squaring H. Working through all four entries gives exactly the identity matrix — confirming H is unitary.

Take the vector 1 plus i, 2, with norm the square root of 6. Applying H gives a new vector, and computing its norm also comes out to exactly the square root of 6 — the same length, unchanged. The Hadamard gate moved the vector but didn't stretch or shrink it at all.

Two physical requirements force every quantum gate to be unitary. Reversibility: quantum evolution must always be undoable, and a unitary matrix's own conjugate transpose is always available as that undo operation. And probability conservation: a valid quantum state has norm 1, and since unitary matrices preserve norm exactly, applying any gate to a valid state always produces another valid state — this is the real reason every gate you'll meet is unitary, not a stylistic choice.

Next lesson puts the inner product and unit length to work together at once — an entire basis that's simultaneously unit-length and mutually perpendicular — and introduces the operator that does exactly what 'picking out one component' means in quantum mechanics.
